occurrences.matched_text: \begin{abstract}Dealers monitor the largest absolute position reached before a review horizon ends. We compare conditional quantile models with historical rules on hourly foreign exchange (FX) positions, weekly New York Fed positions and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) dealer positions, matching histories and update schedules. Historical rules are hard to beat. First, FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% in two periods, but its ranking against a shorter rolling rule changes. Second, in the initial weekly comparisons, historical headroom beats full regression in 34 of 48 New York Fed cases; the better realized historical score wins 29 of 34 CFTC cases. Longer validation improves full regression medians in both reporting systems; CFTC short-history excess falls from 19.3\% to 4.0\%. A benchmark-default gate retains FX gains and improves weekly median performance, but leaves large individual losses. Third, lower scores need not mean lower limit costs: higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor regression in CFTC. Costs are illustrative, and the evidence is retrospective; the original FX evaluation period had been inspected beforehand.\end{abstract}

occurrences.matched_text: \begin{abstract}Dealers monitor the largest absolute position reached before a review horizon ends. We compare conditional quantile models with historical rules on hourly foreign exchange (FX) positions, weekly New York Fed positions and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) dealer positions, matching histories and update schedules. Historical rules are hard to beat. First, FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% in two periods, but its ranking against a shorter rolling rule changes. Second, in the initial weekly comparisons, historical headroom beats full regression in 34 of 48 New York Fed cases; the better realized historical score wins 29 of 34 CFTC cases. Longer validation improves full regression medians in both reporting systems; CFTC short-history excess falls from 19.3\% to 4.0\%. A benchmark-default gate retains FX gains and improves weekly median performance, but leaves large individual losses. Third, lower scores need not mean lower limit costs: higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor regression in CFTC. Costs are illustrative, and the evidence is retrospective; the original FX evaluation period had been inspected beforehand.\end{abstract}

occurrences.matched_text: \begin{abstract}Dealers monitor the largest absolute position reached before a review horizon ends. We compare conditional quantile models with historical rules on hourly foreign exchange (FX) positions, weekly New York Fed positions and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) dealer positions, matching histories and update schedules. Historical rules are hard to beat. First, FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% in two periods, but its ranking against a shorter rolling rule changes. Second, in the initial weekly comparisons, historical headroom beats full regression in 34 of 48 New York Fed cases; the better realized historical score wins 29 of 34 CFTC cases. Longer validation improves full regression medians in both reporting systems; CFTC short-history excess falls from 19.3\% to 4.0\%. A benchmark-default gate retains FX gains and improves weekly median performance, but leaves large individual losses. Third, lower scores need not mean lower limit costs: higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor regression in CFTC. Costs are illustrative, and the evidence is retrospective; the original FX evaluation period had been inspected beforehand.\end{abstract}

current_anchor.matched_text: A fixed extension, committed locally before calculation and uploaded publicly afterward, examines the short-history pattern across 17 CFTC aggregate dealer-position markets. Its fixed horizon is six weeks. The 52- and 260-week results were already known and are reused unchanged; only the 520-week forecasts were new. Both prewritten low-history screens pass: QR4 loses to its matched rolling reference in 15 of 17 cells and QR33 in 29 of 34. The high-history QR4 screen fails, because 10 of 17 wins (58.8\%) fall below the fixed 60\% rule; strict improvement over all three windows holds in only 6 of 17 markets. Full regression has no prewritten high-region cell, leaving its high-history screen untestable. The primary verdict is therefore partial support. These dependent aggregate-market counts describe transport of a fixed prediction; they do not establish a generally sufficient financial history, a causal estimation-cost mechanism, or dealer-level replication. Supplement Section S39 gives all decision screens and counterexamples.
